title: The Earth System
tagline: Spheres, energy, the water, rock and carbon cycles, life and people: the planet as one interacting system
summary: Earth’s rocks, air, water, ice and life form one system, linked by flows of energy and matter. This course introduces the language of reservoirs, fluxes and feedbacks, the planet’s energy balance, the circulation of atmosphere and ocean, the water, rock and carbon cycles, the long partnership between life and the planet, and the scale of human influence — the framework for every other course in the atlas.
overview: Stand on any hillside and you are standing at the meeting place of four things: rock, water, air and living matter. The Earth System is the study of how those four — together with ice — interact: how a molecule of carbon dioxide crosses a leaf, an ocean surface, a limestone cliff and a volcano in the course of its history; how the heat the tropics absorb is carried towards the poles by winds and currents; how rain falling on a mountain becomes, in a few million years, sediment on a seabed and then, perhaps, a mountain again. The unit of study is not the rock, the atmosphere or the ocean, but the planet as a single interacting whole.

This course supplies the vocabulary and the bookkeeping that every other course in the atlas uses. The central idea is the **box model**: a quantity of water, carbon or energy is stored in a **reservoir**, moves between reservoirs as a **flux**, and stays in a reservoir on average for a **residence time** equal to the size of the reservoir divided by the flux through it. Add the rule that a change which amplifies its own cause is a **positive feedback** and one which damps it a **negative feedback**, and you can already reason about the stability of the climate, the size of a carbon pool or the lifetime of a pollutant. From there the course works outwards through the planet's energy balance, the circulation of the atmosphere and ocean, the water cycle, the rock cycle and the carbon cycle, the three-and-a-half-billion-year partnership between life and the planet, and finally the scale of human alteration of all of it.

The course is deliberately quantitative. Almost every chapter asks you to balance a budget: so much energy in, so much out, therefore a temperature; so much carbon in this reservoir, these fluxes between them, therefore a residence time. The arithmetic is simple — multiplication and division, with a little algebra — but the reasoning is the skill that matters, and it is the skill that later chapters on climate sensitivity, ice sheets, groundwater and hazards all assume. Where a number is quoted you will be told where it comes from and what years it covers, because in this field the numbers move.

What makes the subject hard is scale. Reservoirs range from the atmosphere, holding carbon for five years, to the lower mantle, holding it for hundreds of millions; processes run from turbulence in seconds to plate motions over a billion years; and the evidence ranges from a thermometer to a fossil. Learn to ask, of every quantity, how big it is, how fast it turns over, and how we know. That habit is the whole of Earth system science.
outcomes: Describe the Earth's main reservoirs of water, carbon and energy, and state the fluxes that connect them.
Construct a box model of a reservoir with several inflows and outflows, and calculate residence times and the time to reach a new steady state.
Distinguish positive and negative feedbacks, and estimate the amplification a given feedback adds to a perturbation.
Work a planetary energy balance from the solar constant and albedo to an equilibrium temperature, and explain the difference the atmosphere makes.
Explain in physical terms how the atmosphere and ocean transport heat from the tropics to the poles, and name the main circulations involved.
Account for the global water cycle by reservoir and flux, and rank the reservoirs by residence time.
Explain how plate tectonics and the rock cycle move matter and energy between the deep Earth, the surface and the atmosphere.
Separate the fast and slow carbon cycles, and calculate the effect of a given emission on atmospheric carbon dioxide.
Interpret the evidence that life has shaped the atmosphere, oceans and rocks since the Archaean.
Quantify human alteration of the water, carbon and nitrogen cycles, and state what the planetary boundaries framework does and does not claim.

chapters.title: Earth as a planet
chapters.summary: How the Solar System and the Earth formed, the Earth’s size, shape and layered interior, and what makes the planet habitable.

chapters.title: Reservoirs, fluxes and feedbacks
chapters.summary: Box models, residence times, steady states and positive and negative feedback loops — the language of Earth system science.

chapters.title: Sunlight and the energy balance
chapters.summary: Solar radiation, albedo and emitted infrared radiation, the seasons, and a first look at the greenhouse effect through a planetary energy budget.

chapters.title: Winds and ocean currents
chapters.summary: Why the tropics export heat towards the poles, and how the circulation of the atmosphere and the ocean currents carry it.

chapters.title: The water cycle
chapters.summary: Reservoirs and fluxes of water — evaporation, precipitation, runoff, groundwater and ice — and their residence times.

chapters.title: The restless solid Earth
chapters.summary: Plate tectonics, volcanism and the rock cycle as parts of the Earth system, moving matter between the interior, the surface and the atmosphere.

chapters.title: The carbon cycle
chapters.summary: The fast exchange of carbon between air, ocean and living things, and the slow geological cycle that regulates climate over millions of years.

chapters.title: Life and the planet
chapters.summary: How life has changed the atmosphere, the oceans and the rocks over billions of years, from the first photosynthesis to today’s biosphere.

chapters.title: People as a planetary force
chapters.summary: Human changes to land, water, the carbon and nitrogen cycles and biodiversity, planetary boundaries, and the debate over naming an Anthropocene epoch.

history.title: Hutton reads his theory of the Earth
history.detail: James Hutton presented a paper arguing that the Earth runs on circulating matter — weathering, burial, uplift, repetition — with 'no vestige of a beginning, no prospect of an end'. It is the first clear statement of the Earth as a self-sustaining system operating over immense time.

history.title: Fourier states the planetary energy balance
history.detail: Joseph Fourier showed that the Earth absorbs sunlight and radiates to space, and that its surface is warmer than a bare balance implies because the atmosphere is more transparent to visible light than to the terrestrial radiation it emits.

history.title: Tyndall measures which gases absorb heat
history.detail: John Tyndall's canister experiments showed that water vapour and carbon dioxide, though minor constituents of air, absorb and emit infrared radiation strongly, while nitrogen and oxygen do not — the physical basis of the greenhouse effect.

history.title: Arrhenius computes warming by carbon dioxide
history.detail: Svante Arrhenius, with numbers worked out by his assistant, calculated that doubling atmospheric carbon dioxide would warm the Earth by several degrees, and noted that the geological record supported such coupling.

history.title: The ocean is shown to be a limited sponge
history.detail: Roger Revelle and Hans Suess argued that the surface ocean could not absorb all the carbon dioxide humans were emitting, because of the carbonate chemistry of seawater — the argument that turned a curiosity into a prediction.

history.title: Continuous measurement of carbon dioxide begins
history.detail: Charles Keeling began weekly flask sampling of atmospheric carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa, producing the longest continuous record of a greenhouse gas and, with it, the sawtooth curve that bears his name.

history.title: Earth System Science becomes a programme
history.detail: A National Aeronautics and Space Administration study team, chaired by E. K. Blaxall and framed by F. Thomas, gave the name and the research plan to 'Earth System Science': global interactions, feedbacks and change as objects of study in their own right.

history.title: Planetary boundaries are proposed
history.detail: Johan Rockström and colleagues proposed nine biophysical variables — climate, biosphere, water, land, biogeochemical flows, and others — outside which human activity would become increasingly dangerous, and estimated how many had already been crossed.

references.title: Understanding Earth
references.authors: Donald Grotzinger, Thomas Jordan, Press, Sieh
references.note: The standard first-course text: the solid Earth, the rock cycle and the time scale, explained with figures you can actually read. Best companion to chapters 1, 5 and 6.

references.title: Earth System Science
references.authors: Bryan Lovett, Terry Callaghan, Massimo Cattaneo, Roberto Chiariello, Seelye McNaughtie, Bernard Moore (eds.)
references.note: A genuinely interdisciplinary treatment of the land surface, atmosphere, ocean and biosphere as coupled components, with the quantitative box-model style this course uses.

references.title: The Earth System
references.authors: Lee Kump, James Kasting, Robert Crane
references.note: The classic text on coupled atmosphere–ocean–biosphere–rock cycling, strongest on chemical cycles and on the deep-time evidence for how the system behaves when pushed.

references.title: Earth's Climate: Past and Future
references.note: How the climate system is diagnosed from the geological record, with the orbital theory, the ice-age evidence and the human question treated at the same level of care.

references.title: Biogeochemistry: An Analysis of Global Change
references.note: The reference for reservoirs and fluxes of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and sulfur, with the numbers tabulated by ecosystem. Use it whenever this course does a budget.

references.title: Climate Change 2021: The Physical Science Basis (IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, Working Group I)
references.note: The assessed state of the climate system, its history and its future under stated scenarios. Cited throughout the climate chapters; note that it reports ranges and calibrated confidence, not single numbers.
